questions.q: Name the four pigments separated by paper chromatography of a green leaf extract, and state the colour each appears on the chromatogram.
questions.a: The four pigments are: chlorophyll a (bright or blue-green), chlorophyll b (yellow-green), xanthophylls (yellow), and carotenoids (yellow to yellow-orange). A wrong answer (e.g., listing only chlorophyll, or confusing carotene with xanthophyll colours) reveals the student has memorised "chlorophyll is green" from earlier classes but hasn't grasped that leaf colour results from a pigment mixture, and that chromatography separates them based on solubility and adsorption differences – a key Class 11 analytical skill.

questions.q: Explain why the action spectrum of photosynthesis does not perfectly overlap with the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a alone, even though chlorophyll a is the primary photosynthetic pigment.
questions.a: The action spectrum shows photosynthesis rate at each wavelength, while chlorophyll a absorption spectrum shows only its light absorption. Accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids) absorb at wavelengths where chlorophyll a absorbs poorly (e.g., 450–500 nm, 640–650 nm) and transfer energy to chlorophyll a, so photosynthesis occurs at those wavelengths too. A wrong answer stating "they overlap completely" or "carotenoids don't participate" reveals the misconception that only chlorophyll a matters, ignoring the antenna function of accessory pigments – a classic Class 10 oversimplification.

questions.q: A student extracts pigments from a variegated leaf (green and white patches) and runs paper chromatography. The green patch shows four bands; the white patch shows only two yellow-orange bands. Identify the two pigments in the white patch and explain their presence.
questions.a: The white patch contains only xanthophylls and carotenoids (the two yellow-orange bands). These pigments are present in all plastids, including non-photosynthetic ones, and are more stable than chlorophylls. In the absence of chlorophyll synthesis (due to mutation or lack of light), the carotenoids remain visible. A wrong answer (e.g., "no pigments in white patch" or "chlorophyll a and b are there but colourless") reveals confusion between pigment absence and chlorophyll-specific absence, and ignorance that carotenoids are universal in plastids – a gap from Class 9 plastid types (c9_bio_ch1_10).

questions.q: Compare the organisation of pigments in Photosystem I and Photosystem II. How does the reaction centre chlorophyll a differ between them, and why is this difference functionally significant?
questions.a: Both photosystems have hundreds of pigment molecules (chlorophyll a, b, carotenoids) forming light-harvesting complexes (antennae) bound to proteins. The difference: PS I reaction centre chlorophyll a (P700) absorbs maximally at 700 nm; PS II reaction centre chlorophyll a (P680) absorbs at 680 nm. This 20 nm shift tunes each photosystem to slightly different light qualities, enabling sequential excitation in the Z-scheme: PS II (680 nm) excites first, passes electrons uphill, then PS I (700 nm) re-excites them to reduce NADP+. A wrong answer missing the wavelength distinction or the sequential role reveals failure to connect pigment structure to electron transport energetics – a prerequisite for node c11_bio_cbse_11_003.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: "Since chlorophyll a absorbs maximally in blue (430 nm) and red (662 nm) light, plants grow best under pure blue or pure red LED lights; green light (500–570 nm) is useless for photosynthesis because chlorophyll reflects it."
questions.a: The statement is partially incorrect. While chlorophyll a absorbs poorly in green, accessory pigments (chlorophyll b, carotenoids) absorb some green light and transfer energy to chlorophyll a. Moreover, green light penetrates deeper into leaf mesophyll, driving photosynthesis in lower chloroplast layers. Pure red/blue LEDs can cause photoinhibition and unbalanced growth; full-spectrum light including green gives higher total photosynthesis. A wrong evaluation accepting the statement reveals the "green light is wasted" misconception from oversimplified Class 10 action spectrum graphs, ignoring leaf optics and pigment diversity.

questions.q: Give the correct order of steps in the prism-and-bacteria experiment that shows where photosynthesis is maximal.
questions.a: The experiment runs: (1) Pass white light through a prism to spread a spectrum over a filament of the alga (2) Suspend aerobic bacteria in the drop with the alga (3) Wait and observe where the bacteria accumulate most densely (4) Read the dense clusters in the blue and red regions as the zones of highest oxygen evolution and photosynthesis. A wrong answer that expects bacteria evenly everywhere shows the student has missed that bacteria track oxygen, making them living indicators of the photosynthetic rate across wavelengths.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: ______ in higher plants is a physico-chemical process occurring in chloroplasts where green plants convert light energy into chemical energy by using carbon dioxide and water to synthesise carbohydrates, with oxygen released as a by-product.
Fill in the blank: ______ a spinach leaf (palak) held against sunlight – you see deep green, but notice the younger leaves are lighter green while older ones may yellow.
What is Photosynthesis in higher plants? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Photosynthesis in higher plants is a physico-chemical process occurring in chloroplasts where green plants convert light energy into chemical energy by using carbon dioxide and water to synthesise carbohydrates, with oxygen released as a by-product.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can label chloroplast ultrastructure (grana, stroma, thylakoid, stroma lamellae) in an electron micrograph, explain why chlorophyll a is the primary pigment using absorption and action spectra, and describe how accessory pigments expand the spectrum of usable light while protecting chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation.
